explanations.answer: Come together to wage war on Israel
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The kings of the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites and the rest came together to wage war against Joshua and Israel. The list runs from the hill country all the way to the coast. That's six different peoples gathered around one plan, like a whole office actually showing up for the same meeting.

explanations.answer: Pack up and leave the land for good
explanations.explanation: Nobody's loading a moving truck here, friend. The text says the kings came together to wage war against Joshua and Israel. Every one of them heard the news, and every one of them reached for a fight instead of a suitcase.

explanations.answer: Build new walls around all their cities
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions new walls. It says the kings came together to wage war against Joshua and Israel. And I think walls weren't a hot item right then, since Jericho's wall fell flat (Joshua 6:20).
Yep, the text says the people of Gibeon acted deceptively. The sacks, the wineskins, the sandals and the clothes were all part of the act. They showed up dressed for a trip they never took.
Close in spirit, baker, because walking into a camp takes nerve. But the text says they acted deceptively. The worn-out gear wasn't a show of courage, it was a costume.

Careless is when you leave the house without your keys. These folks packed patched sandals, cracked wineskins and threadbare clothes. That's a whole wardrobe of props, and the text says they acted deceptively.
Not quite, friend. The text says their whole supply of bread was dry and moldy. Fresh and soft bread would have ruined the whole costume. Nobody sells a long trip with a warm loaf in the sack.

Right, baker. Their whole supply of bread was dry and moldy. Fresh and soft would have ruined the look they were going for. Even the stalest cookie I ever pressed would have been fresher than that sack.

explanations.answer: They wonder if the Hivites live nearby
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The men of Israel say, “Perhaps you dwell near us. How can we make a treaty with you?” They don't say yes right away. They ask the question out loud.

explanations.answer: They agree to a treaty right away
explanations.explanation: Not yet, friend. The treaty comes later in the passage. First, the men of Israel say, “Perhaps you dwell near us. How can we make a treaty with you?”

explanations.answer: They tell the Hivites to go home
explanations.explanation: No shooing here, friend. The men of Israel ask, “Perhaps you dwell near us. How can we make a treaty with you?” They don't send anyone off. They poke at the story first. I think those words sound like Israel isn't sure yet.

explanations.answer: Because of the fame of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's what they say, baker. They tell Joshua they came “because of the fame of the LORD your God.” Keep in mind, this is the Gibeonites talking, and their story about a distant land isn't true. They make the LORD's name the headline of their speech.

explanations.answer: Because a famine drove them out
explanations.explanation: The text has no famine here. The Gibeonites say they came because of the LORD's fame. Hunger isn't in their story, friend, though the moldy bread might make you think it should be.

explanations.answer: Because enemies chased them from home
explanations.explanation: Nobody's chasing anybody in their speech. They say they came “because of the fame of the LORD your God.” Their reason is the reports they heard about Him.

Close, friend, but look at what they actually say to Joshua. They talk about Egypt, and about Sihon, king of Heshbon, and Og, king of Bashan, the two kings of the Amorites beyond the Jordan. Jericho and Ai don't come up in that speech. Those two cities show up back in verse 3, as the news the Gibeonites had heard.

Right, baker. They name Egypt, plus Sihon, king of Heshbon, and Og, king of Bashan, the two kings of the Amorites beyond the Jordan. Jericho and Ai are missing from the speech. Funny what a person leaves out when they're telling a story.

Yes, baker. They say their clothes and sandals are “…worn out from our very long journey.” Cracked wineskins, patched sandals and threadbare clothes are what they wanted Joshua to see. The distance behind that picture was not true (Joshua 9:16). It's a very convincing look for a trip that never happened.
No battles in their story, friend. They say their clothes and sandals are worn out from their very long journey. A trip is what they want Joshua to picture.
Nobody mentions a season here. The Gibeonites say their clothes and sandals are worn out from their very long journey. There's no weather report in this story, baker.

explanations.answer: Seek the counsel of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The men of Israel sampled the provisions but did not seek the counsel of the LORD. They checked the bread and skipped asking Him. Sometimes the thing we leave out is the whole story.
They did ask questions, friend. The men of Israel said, “Perhaps you dwell near us.” and Joshua asked, “Who are you and where have you come from?” What they skipped was asking the LORD.
They listened, baker. The Gibeonites told them all about the long trip, the fame of the LORD and the moldy bread. What the men of Israel did not do was seek the counsel of the LORD.

explanations.answer: Makes a treaty of peace to let them live
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Joshua made a treaty of peace with them to let them live. Right before that, the men of Israel sampled their provisions but did not seek the counsel of the LORD. The leaders of the congregation swore an oath to them too. That treaty is going to matter.

explanations.answer: Sends spies out to check their story
explanations.explanation: Spies don't show up in this scene, friend. The text says the men of Israel sampled their provisions but did not seek the counsel of the LORD, and then Joshua made a treaty of peace with them (Joshua 9:14-15). Checking the story with scouts isn't mentioned. The Gibeonites do say their own elders told them to go meet Israel (Joshua 9:11), but that's a different trip.

explanations.answer: Sends them away with nothing at all
explanations.explanation: They don't leave empty-handed, baker. Joshua made a treaty of peace with them to let them live. The Gibeonites got what they came for.

That's right, baker. The leaders of the congregation swore an oath to them, too. So the treaty had Joshua's agreement and the leaders' oath behind it. Keep an eye on that oath, because it matters a lot.
Not quite, friend. The text says the leaders of the congregation swore an oath to the Gibeonites. Joshua made the treaty, and the leaders put their oath on it. That oath is going to matter.

Not so, friend. Three days after the treaty, the Israelites learned the Gibeonites were neighbors, living among them. The very distant land was never there. That's one short trip for such a long story.

Right, baker. Three days after the treaty, the Israelites learned that the Gibeonites were neighbors, living among them. The faraway land was a story they told. A very long journey that ends up next door is quite a trip.

That's not what happens, friend. Israel reaches the cities, but the Israelites did not attack them. The leaders had sworn an oath to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. The whole congregation grumbled against the leaders, but the oath is the reason the text gives.

Yes, baker. The Israelites did not attack them. The text gives the reason: the leaders had sworn an oath to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. The congregation grumbled against the leaders, but no attack came.

explanations.answer: The leaders swore an oath to them by the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The Israelites did not attack, “…because the leaders of the congregation had sworn an oath to them by the LORD, the God of Israel.” The oath was sworn by the LORD. That's what stopped them at the gates.

explanations.answer: The Gibeonite armies were far too strong
explanations.explanation: The text never says anything about Gibeonite armies. It says Israel held back because the leaders had sworn an oath to them by the LORD. The reason is the oath, friend, not a battle plan.

explanations.answer: The Gibeonites paid Israel to leave them alone
explanations.explanation: No payment in this passage, baker. The text says the leaders had sworn an oath to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. That's why Israel held back.

That's right, baker. The leaders say they will let the Gibeonites live, “…so that no wrath will fall on us because of the oath we swore to them.” They took the oath seriously. They didn't want to break it.
Shame isn't the word the leaders use, friend. They say they'll let the Gibeonites live so that no wrath will fall on them because of the oath they swore. It's a serious word for a serious promise.
No famine in this speech, baker. The leaders say they'll let the Gibeonites live so that no wrath will fall on them because of the oath they swore. They were worried about the oath.

That's the job, baker. The leaders say, “Let them live, but let them be woodcutters and water carriers for the whole congregation.” They keep their promise to let the Gibeonites live. Wood and water are chores like laundry: finished today, needed again tomorrow.
No night watch in this passage, friend. The leaders say the Gibeonites will be woodcutters and water carriers for the whole congregation. It's a lot of wood and water.
No sheep here, baker. The leaders say the Gibeonites will be woodcutters and water carriers for the whole congregation. They live, and they work.

Yes, baker. Joshua asks why they deceived him, since they said they lived far away when they lived right there among Israel. Then he says, "Now therefore you are under a curse…" (Joshua 9:23). He means it, and the job that follows is a lasting one. I think this part is heavy.

Not a blessing, friend. Joshua calls it a curse, and the job that comes with it has no end date. The Gibeonites will cut wood and carry water for the house of his God (Joshua 9:23). I think this part is heavy, and it's about as far from a blessing as you can get.
No prizes in this scene, baker. Joshua tells the Gibeonites they are under a curse. It comes right after he asks why they deceived him.

explanations.answer: They greatly feared for their lives
explanations.explanation: That's what they say, baker. They tell Joshua they were told the LORD commanded His servant Moses to give Israel all the land. So, in their words, “…we greatly feared for our lives because of you…” That fear is the reason they give for the trick.

explanations.answer: They wanted to spy on Israel
explanations.explanation: Spying isn't what they say, friend. They tell Joshua they were told the LORD commanded Moses to give Israel all the land and wipe out all its inhabitants (Joshua 9:24). That's why they say they feared for their lives. Not a word about spying in their answer.

explanations.answer: They hoped to take Israel's land
explanations.explanation: That's not their story, friend. The reason they give is fear. They say they knew about the command to give Israel the land and wipe out everyone living in it, so they worried for their own lives (Joshua 9:24). Grabbing Israel's land never comes up in what they tell Joshua.

explanations.answer: Delivers them so Israel doesn't kill them
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Joshua delivered them from the hands of the Israelites, and they did not kill the Gibeonites. The congregation had grumbled earlier, but the Gibeonites got through it alive. That's a hard outcome and a merciful one.

explanations.answer: Drives them out of the land for good
explanations.explanation: No exile in this story, friend. Joshua delivered them from the hands of the Israelites, and they did not kill the Gibeonites. They stayed, and they went to work.

explanations.answer: Hands them over to the angry congregation
explanations.explanation: It goes the other way, baker. The congregation grumbled against the leaders, but Joshua delivered the Gibeonites from the hands of the Israelites. They did not kill the Gibeonites.

That's right, baker. On that day Joshua made them woodcutters and water carriers for the congregation of the LORD and for the altar at the place He would choose. The work reaches all the way to the altar. And the text says they're still at it to this day.
The text says it plainly, friend. Joshua made them woodcutters and water carriers for the congregation of the LORD and for the altar at the place He would choose. Both are in the verse.
